extracted.intended_audience: mathematically literate readers (advanced undergraduates, graduate students, and research mathematicians)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological standards for constructing and judging mathematical arguments, proofs, and related mathematical objects (e.g., computer-assisted proofs, fractal dimension definitions, minimal-surface behavior).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reducible configuration
rubrics_metrics.description: A configuration is reducible if the four-colourability of any map that contains it can be proved provided a smaller map is four-colourable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: shrink a triangular region to a point; if the resulting map (one region fewer) can be 4‑coloured, then so can the original because the triangle abuts only three regions. Squares are reducible; Kempe thought pentagons were reducible but was wrong. A minimal criminal (minimal counterexample) cannot contain a reducible configuration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unavoidable set
rubrics_metrics.description: An unavoidable set is a set of configurations with the property that any map must contain a configuration in that set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy for the Four Colour Theorem: find an unavoidable set composed entirely of reducible configurations. Kempe proved {triangle, square, pentagon} is unavoidable but failed on reducibility of pentagon. Heesch estimated about 10,000 configurations might be needed; Appel and Haken constructed an unavoidable set of ~2000 configurations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heesch's discharging method
rubrics_metrics.description: A technique for proving that certain configurations must occur by assigning and redistributing 'charge' among regions according to rules, then analysing the resulting charge distributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example rule: split the charge on any pentagon into equal parts and transfer to neighbors except triangles, squares, and pentagons. Analysing general features of charge distributions can show certain configurations must occur (otherwise charge 'leaks away'). More complicated recipes produce more complicated unavoidable lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-assisted proof acceptability
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria by which an argument relying on enormous computation can be considered a valid mathematical proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points: the proof strategy must make logical sense and 'hang together'; details should be checkable in principle by humans; the computer program must be correct; components obtained by hand (e.g., unavoidable set) increase confidence; random 'spot tests' and independent checks bolster trust; consensus of experts matters. Philosophical objections exist but practicing mathematicians accept long or computer-aided proofs when the strategy and checks are sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal-criminal (contradiction) proof strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof by contradiction via minimal counterexample: assume a minimal criminal (smallest counterexample) exists and show it cannot, by structural properties, avoid a reducible configuration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If every minimal criminal must contain a reducible configuration, and every configuration in an unavoidable set is reducible, then no minimal criminal can exist, yielding the theorem. This is an organizing logical strategy used in the Four Colour Theorem approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scaling (fractal) dimension definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The scaling dimension d of a set that can be assembled from c copies each scaled by a factor a is d = (log c)/(log a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cantor set: a=3, c=2 gives d = log 2 / log 3 ≈ 0.6309; Sierpinski gasket doubled by 3 copies gives d = log 3 / log 2 ≈ 1.58496. This explains non-integer dimensions and why the quantity is called a 'dimension' — it agrees with usual dimension for nice sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hausdorff-Besicovitch (fractal) dimension as empirical/theoretical criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The fractal (Hausdorff-Besicovitch) dimension is a precise quantity usable in applications because it can be measured experimentally and compared with theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: it measures 'how well the set fills space' or 'how rough the set is' (e.g., Cantor set lies between point and line). The fractal dimension may be non-integer; sometimes it coincides with scaling dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topological invariants for knots/links
rubrics_metrics.description: Topological invariants are numbers or more complicated mathematical objects that do not change under continuous deformations and are used to decide whether two knots or links are equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A central problem is to find efficient invariants to distinguish inequivalent knots; the Jones polynomial is highlighted as a remarkable new method for this purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic complexity classification (polynomial vs non-polynomial)
rubrics_metrics.description: A problem is 'easy' if there exists an algorithm whose running time grows no faster than a fixed power of n (polynomial time); it is 'hard' if the running time grows non-polynomially (e.g., exponentially).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical meaning: polynomial-time algorithms are usually feasible; non-polynomial often impractical. Examples: addition and multiplication are polynomial-time; enumerating all TSP routes is factorial and thus impractical. There is a continuum between polynomial and exponential where practicality depends on constants and experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardness proof by reductions (NP-completeness/Cook's theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a problem is hard, one must show that any algorithm for it would yield polynomial-time algorithms for a wide class of candidate hard problems; Cook's theorem shows a group of candidate problems (NP) sink or swim together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rough idea: code one problem as a special case of another to show that proving one is hard implies all are hard. NP-complete problems are those representative hard problems; everyone believes NP-complete problems are really hard though it's unproven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steiner ratio conjecture as approximation criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Steiner ratio conjecture concerns the ratio of Steiner minimal tree length to spanning (minimum spanning tree) length; bounds on this ratio justify replacing a hard optimization (Steiner) by an easier one (spanning) without large loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical progress improved lower bounds on the ratio; Du and Hwang proved the conjecture using a reduction to lattice networks and a game-theory formulation introducing convexity. Computational verification for small n provided evidence prior to theoretical advances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plateau's principles for soap films (shape standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plateau's three principles describing soap-film forms: (1) they consist of a finite number of flat or smoothly curved surfaces smoothly joined together; (2) surfaces meet only in two ways: exactly three surfaces meet along a smooth curve, or four surfaces meet at a point; (3) when three surfaces meet their angles are 120°, and when four meet the corner angles are approximately 109°.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Almgren and Taylor (1976) proved these follow from the single principle that the soap film minimizes total area. The first principle (finiteness) is the most difficult to establish; the other two follow from geometric arguments once finiteness and smoothness are accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation of intersection angles via spherical reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: To deduce local intersection angles of area-minimizing planar surfaces, magnify a small region near an intersection, approximate by planes, intersect with a sphere centered at the intersection, and reduce to minimizing total length of arcs of great circles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spherical version of Steiner's theorem implies arcs meet three at 120°; an exhaustive classification (ten configurations) of great-circle arc systems and checking small deformations yields that only three survive, giving the planar possibilities and the 120°/109° angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric measure theory representation for minimal surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace a geometric surface S by an associated 'measure' that assigns to any region X the area of S inside X; extend this to more complex shapes and define generalized area to enable compactness/limit arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof structure: (1) prove existence of a minimizing measure (straightforward in this framework); (2) use minimality to show the minimizing measure corresponds to a finite system of smooth surfaces. This addresses the hard step of proving finiteness of the actual geometric minimal surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstandard analysis transfer principle and constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonstandard analysis constructs a model R* of the reals that extends R and contains infinitesimals and infinities; every first-order property of R extends naturally to R*, but second-order properties (like the Archimedean axiom) may fail in R*.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions: finite = smaller than some standard real; infinitesimal = smaller than all positive standard reals; infinite = not finite. There is a unique standard part std(x) for each finite hyperreal x (x − std(x) is infinitesimal). This transfer and standard-part machinery allows translating results between R and R* and can make some proofs shorter/more intuitive, at the cost of requiring model-theoretic background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinitesimal definitions of continuity and derivative
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuity and differentiability can be formulated in nonstandard terms: (2) f is continuous at x if f(x+e) is infinitely close to f(x) for all infinitesimal e; (3) f has derivative d at x iff [f(x+Δx)−f(x)]/Δx is infinitely close to d for all infinitesimals Δx.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions formalize Leibniz/Newton-style infinitesimal reasoning rigorously in R* and often produce shorter, more direct proofs than epsilon–delta arguments. They exemplify how nonstandard analysis can mirror classical results with different conceptual machinery.
